claim: Phloem unloading of solutes in Arabidopsis roots occurs through plasmodesmata by a combination of mass flow and diffusion (convective phloem unloading).
source: We used a combination of approaches (non-invasive imaging, 3D-electron microscopy, and mathematical modelling) to show that phloem unloading of solutes in Arabidopsis roots occurs through plasmodesmata by a combination of mass flow and diffusion (convective phloem unloading).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from non-invasive imaging, 3D-electron microscopy, and mathematical modelling as stated in the abstract.

claim: During unloading, solutes and proteins are diverted into the phloem-pole pericycle.
source: During unloading, solutes and proteins are diverted into the phloem-pole pericycle, a tissue connected to the protophloem by a unique class of 'funnel plasmodesmata'.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the abstract and detailed in the results section.

claim: The phloem-pole pericycle is connected to the protophloem by a unique class of 'funnel plasmodesmata'.
source: During unloading, solutes and proteins are diverted into the phloem-pole pericycle, a tissue connected to the protophloem by a unique class of 'funnel plasmodesmata'.
evidence: The claim is supported by ultrastructural analysis showing funnel-shaped plasmodesmata at the PSE-PPP interface.

claim: While solutes are unloaded without restriction, large proteins are released through funnel plasmodesmata in discrete pulses.
source: While solutes are unloaded without restriction, large proteins are released through funnel plasmodesmata in discrete pulses, a phenomenon we refer to as 'batch unloading'.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging experiments showing discrete pulses of protein unloading.

claim: Large proteins remain restricted to the phloem-pole pericycle after unloading.
source: Unlike solutes, these proteins remain restricted to the phloem-pole pericycle.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging showing that large proteins like SEOR-YFP and aequorin-GFP do not move beyond the PPP.

claim: The phloem-pole pericycle has a major role in regulating phloem unloading in roots.
source: Our data demonstrate a major role for the phloem-pole pericycle in regulating phloem unloading in roots.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including structural analysis, unloading kinetics, and callose induction experiments.

claim: Modern agriculture aims to maximize the amounts of carbon-based products allocated to storage organs such as grains and tubers.
source: Modern agriculture aims to maximize the amounts of carbon-based products allocated to storage organs such as grains and tubers, structures that act as carbon 'sinks' for the assimilates delivered by the phloem.
evidence: This is a statement about agricultural practices and goals, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Phloem unloading is a central target for regulating the flux of carbon into sink tissues.
source: The process by which solutes exit the phloem is termed phloem unloading, and is a central target for regulating the flux of carbon into sink tissues (Ham and Lucas, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ham and Lucas, 2014.

claim: Phloem sap contains numerous proteins and RNAs in addition to assimilates.
source: In addition to assimilates, phloem sap also contains numerous proteins and RNAs (Kehr, 2006; Atkins et al., 2011; Batailler et al., 2012; Turnbull and Lopez-Cobollo, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: During differentiation, sieve elements lose most of their cellular components, including their nucleus.
source: During differentiation SEs lose most of their cellular components, including their nucleus (Oparka and Turgeon, 1999; Furuta et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oparka and Turgeon, 1999 and Furuta et al., 2014.

claim: Companion cells support the adjacent enucleate sieve elements throughout their lifespan.
source: Ontogenetically related, metabolically active companion cells (CCs) support the adjacent enucleate SEs throughout their lifespan (Lucas et al., 1996; Pritchard, 1996; van Bel and Knoblauch, 2000; Lalonde et al., 2001; Otero and Helariutta, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The pressure flow model of phloem transport was originally proposed by Münch in 1930.
source: The pressure flow model of phloem transport, originally proposed by Münch (1930), envisages that an osmotically generated pressure differential drives the bulk flow through the SEs that connect photosynthetic tissues (sources) with those in which carbon consumption occurs (sinks).
evidence: The claim is a historical fact supported by citation to Münch, 1930.

claim: Many proteins found in phloem sap, including those with targeting sequences, can move across a graft union and be unloaded near the root tip.
source: In a recent study, Paultre et al. (2016) showed that many proteins, including those with targeting sequences, can move across a graft union and be unloaded near the root tip.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Paultre et al., 2016.

claim: Proteins unloaded near the root tip entered a post-phloem domain beyond which their movement was restricted.
source: Significantly, these proteins entered a post-phloem domain beyond which their movement was restricted.
evidence: The claim is based on findings from Paultre et al., 2016 as referenced in the preceding sentence.

claim: The phloem serves as a network for transmission of chemical and electrical signals.
source: Besides the central function in resource allocation, it is now well established that the phloem also serves as network for transmission of chemical (Kramer and Boyer, 1995a; Mullendore et al., 2015) and electrical (Hedrich et al., 2016) signals.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Phloem unloading in actively growing tissues such as the shoot or root apex occurs through the protophloem.
source: Phloem unloading in actively growing tissues such as the shoot or root apex occurs through the protophloem, a transient tissue that connects the conducting phloem with the receiver cells in sink tissues (Oparka et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Oparka et al., 1994.

claim: Initial investigations of phloem unloading in the root tip of Arabidopsis provided evidence that unloading occurs through plasmodesmata.
source: Initial investigations of phloem unloading in the root tip of Arabidopsis (Oparka et al., 1994, 1995; Wright and Oparka, 1996) provided evidence that unloading occurs through plasmodesmata (PD), the specialized pores that connect plant cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oparka et al., 1994, 1995 and Wright and Oparka, 1996.

claim: Protophloem sieve elements become mature in regions of high assimilate demand while neighboring cells are still differentiating.
source: Protophloem sieve elements (PSEs) become mature in such regions to accommodate this demand while the neighboring cells are still differentiating (Furuta et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Furuta et al., 2014.

claim: Protophloem sieve elements become increasingly elongated until they become inactive in transport and eventually obliterated.
source: Therefore, they become increasingly elongated until they become inactive in transport and eventually obliterated (Erwin and Evert, 1967; Eleftheriou and Tsekos, 1982; Furuta et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In the elongation zone of the root, solutes are transferred laterally from the metaphloem sieve elements to the protophloem sieve elements.
source: In the elongation zone of the root, solutes are transferred laterally from the metaphloem SEs (MSEs) to the PSEs, allowing phloem continuity between source and sink tissues (Stadler et al., 2005; Winter et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stadler et al., 2005 and Winter et al., 1992.

claim: The high-pressure manifold model proposes that a low pressure gradient occurs along the flow path, with a steep drop in pressure between the protophloem sieve elements and surrounding cells in the phloem unloading zone.
source: A currently favored hypothesis of phloem unloading is the 'high-pressure manifold model' proposed by Fisher (2000), recently evaluated by Patrick (2013). A central element of this model is that a low pressure gradient occurs along the flow path, with a steep drop in pressure between the PSEs and surrounding cells in the phloem unloading zone.
evidence: The claim describes a model proposed by Fisher (2000) and evaluated by Patrick (2013).

claim: Recent phloem turgor measurements in morning glory did not support the high-pressure manifold model.
source: Recent phloem turgor measurements in morning glory, however, did not support this model, as the bulk of the pressure is consumed by friction within the SEs, and only small pressure gradients are available for unloading (Knoblauch et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Knoblauch et al., 2016.

claim: The Fisher (2000) model does not explain how both small solutes and macromolecules can leave the phloem simultaneously.
source: The Fisher (2000) model also does not explain how both small solutes and macromolecules can leave the phloem simultaneously.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of the Fisher (2000) model.

claim: The phloem unloading zone in Arabidopsis is amenable to non-invasive imaging.
source: The many unknowns surrounding phloem unloading in plants prompted us to conduct a detailed structure/function study of the terminal PSEs in the phloem unloading zone which, in Arabidopsis, is amenable to non-invasive imaging (Oparka et al., 1994; Knoblauch et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oparka et al., 1994 and Knoblauch et al., 2015.

claim: CFDA is the most widely utilized phloem-mobile probe.
source: Carboxyfluorescein diacetate (CFDA) is the most widely utilized phloem-mobile probe (Oparka et al., 1994; Wright and Oparka, 1996; Knoblauch and van Bel, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies using CFDA.

claim: CFDA is non-fluorescent when applied to source leaves but is subsequently cleaved by endogenous esterases to produce fluorescent, membrane-impermeant, carboxyfluorescein.
source: This probe is non-fluorescent when applied to source leaves but is subsequently cleaved by endogenous esterases to produce fluorescent, membrane-impermeant, carboxyfluorescein (CF; Knoblauch et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Knoblauch et al., 2015.

claim: CFDA characteristically shows preferential movement outwards into the cortex relative to the stele when studied in real time.
source: When studied in real time, the dye characteristically shows preferential movement outwards into the cortex relative to the stele (Figure 1A; see also Oparka et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and citation to Oparka et al., 1994.

claim: Unloading of CFDA in the root tip indicates a symplastic (plasmodesmata-mediated) pathway.
source: Unloading of the dye in the root tip indicates a symplastic (plasmodesmata-mediated) pathway (Oparka et al., 1994; Wright and Oparka, 1996; Knoblauch et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Cells in the unloading zone sequester CFDA rapidly into their vacuoles where it becomes trapped.
source: The cells in the unloading zone sequester the dye rapidly into their vacuoles where it becomes trapped.
evidence: The claim is based on observations described in the text and supported by Wright and Oparka, 1996 as cited in the following sentence.

claim: Esculin is a naturally fluorescent, glucosylated coumarin derivative recently introduced as phloem-mobile probe.
source: Esculin is a naturally fluorescent, glucosylated coumarin derivative recently introduced as phloem-mobile probe (Knoblauch et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Knoblauch et al., 2015.

claim: Esculin is loaded into the phloem by the sucrose transporter, SUC2, in the companion cells of source tissues.
source: Unlike CFDA, it is loaded into the phloem by the sucrose transporter, SUC2, in the CCs of source tissues (Gora et al., 2012; Knoblauch et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gora et al., 2012 and Knoblauch et al., 2015.

claim: Sequestration of esculin is minimal and occurs only when high concentrations of the probe are applied.
source: Sequestration of this probe is minimal and occurs only when high concentrations of the probe are applied (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Esculin did not enter differentiating protophloem sieve elements that were symplastically isolated from the rest of the protophloem file.
source: Esculin did not enter differentiating PSEs that were symplastically isolated from the rest of the protophloem file.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from time-lapse movies described in the text.

claim: Once the nuclear membrane started to degenerate, the sieve-plate pores opened rapidly, allowing esculin to enter the cell.
source: Once the nuclear membrane started to degenerate the sieve-plate pores opened rapidly, allowing esculin to enter the cell, which then became an integral member of the protophloem-unloading zone (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 1D and E.

claim: The degeneration of the nucleus and the opening of the sieve-plate pores are closely related events that lead to incorporation of PSE zero into the phloem-unloading zone.
source: Our data suggest that nucleate, differentiating PSEs are isolated from the translocation stream. However, the degeneration of the nucleus and the opening of the sieve-plate pores are closely related events that lead to incorporation of PSE zero into the phloem-unloading zone.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental observations described.

claim: Phloem flow velocities in the terminal region of the root (basipetal to the unloading zone) are in the range of 25 µm/s.
source: Phloem flow velocities in the terminal region of the root (basipetal to the unloading zone) are in the range of 25 µm/s (Froelich et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Froelich et al., 2011.

claim: Deceleration of phloem flow started at about 300–400 µm behind PSE zero.
source: To define the size of the unloading zone, we measured flow velocity along the phloem files and found that deceleration started at about 300–400 µm behind PSE zero (this dimension varied slightly, even within the two sieve tube files in the same root tip; Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow velocity measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: The phloem of the root is subdivided into distinct structural and functional domains.
source: Our data revealed that the phloem of the root is subdivided into distinct structural and functional domains.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing different zones with different functions.

claim: Arabidopsis roots grow at speeds of about 100–150 µm per hour.
source: Arabidopsis roots grow at speeds of about 100–150 µm per hour (Beemster and Baskin, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Beemster and Baskin, 1998.

claim: After the sieve-plate pores open, a single protophloem sieve element in the phloem unloading zone is active in unloading for only about 2–4 hr.
source: Consequently, after the sieve-plate pores open, a single PSE in the phloem unloading zone is active in unloading for only about 2–4 hr.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the root growth rate and the dimensions of the unloading zone.

claim: Callose is deposited in the neck region of plasmodesmata and restricts the size exclusion limit of the pore in response to various stimuli.
source: Callose is deposited in the neck region of plasmodesmata and restricts the size exclusion limit of the pore in response to various stimuli (Luna et al., 2011; Nakashima et al., 2003; Radford et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: At the junction of the phloem unloading zone with the phloem translocation zone, callose deposits on the protophloem sieve element wall increased in number.
source: At the junction of the phloem unloading zone with the phloem translocation zone, callose deposits on the PSE wall increased in number (Figure 3E) until significant parts of the PSE walls were covered in callose (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: Deposition of callose along the lateral walls of protophloem sieve elements in the protophloem translocation zone correlated with the reduction in flow observed in dye-loading experiments.
source: This deposition of callose along the lateral walls of PSEs in the protophloem translocation zone correlated with the reduction in flow we observed in dye-loading experiments and may provide a structural basis for the functional isolation of this zone.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the correlation between callose deposition and flow reduction.

claim: A large number of macromolecules including nucleic acids and proteins occur in various amounts in the translocation stream.
source: As well as sugars and amino acids, a large number of macromolecules including nucleic acids, and proteins occur in various amounts in the translocation stream (Fukumorita and Chino, 1982; Kehr, 2006; Turnbull and Lopez-Cobollo, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In Arabidopsis, the root protophloem file is surrounded by five distinct cell files.
source: In Arabidopsis, the root protophloem file is surrounded by five distinct cell files (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM images shown in Figures 4A and B.

claim: Small probes of the dimensions of sugars and amino acids (CFDA, esculin), and small proteins (GFP) move from cell to cell throughout the entire root tip without noticeable barriers.
source: Small probes of the dimensions of sugars and amino acids (CFDA, esculin), and small proteins (GFP) move from cell to cell throughout the entire root tip without noticeable barriers (Figure 1; Oparka et al., 1994; Stadler et al., 2005; Wright and Oparka, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations and citations to multiple studies.

claim: Translocated proteins of companion cell origin are restricted to cells immediately adjacent to the mature protophloem file.
source: However, translocated proteins of CC origin, are restricted to cells immediately adjacent to the mature protophloem file (Stadler et al., 2005; Paultre et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stadler et al., 2005 and Paultre et al., 2016.

claim: SEOR-YFP signal was confined to the two large phloem-pole pericycle cells that abut the protophloem sieve element files.
source: We used resin embedding of the phloem-unloading zone (Bell et al., 2013) to localize the YFP signal in transverse sections of the root. The YFP signal was confined to the two large PPP cells that abut the PSE files (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 4D and E.

claim: Phloem unloading of SEOR-YFP into companion cells was not detected, only into the phloem-pole pericycle.
source: Using a fluorescent marker for CC nuclei (Zhang et al., 2008) we were unable to detect phloem unloading of SEOR-YFP into CCs, only into the PPP (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 4H and I.

claim: Most models of phloem unloading assume that the exit of macromolecules occurs through companion cells.
source: This result was unexpected as most models of phloem unloading assume that the exit of macromolecules occurs through CCs (Patrick, 1997; Thorne, 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Patrick, 1997 and Thorne, 1985.

claim: SEOR-YFP protein, synthesized in sieve elements of the shoot, is unloaded from protophloem sieve elements into the phloem-pole pericycle.
source: 10 days after grafting, the roots of the grafted plants were indistinguishable from those of the native SEOR-YFP line (Figure 4I,J), demonstrating that SEOR-YFP protein, synthesized in SEs of the shoot, is unloaded from PSEs into the PPP.
evidence: The claim is supported by grafting experiments shown in Figures 4I and J.

claim: Unloading of large probes (GFP 27 kDa and above) did not occur at a constant rate but was suddenly released into the adjoining phloem-pole pericycle cells in distinct pulses.
source: Time-lapse movies revealed that unloading of large probes (GFP 27 kDa and above) did not occur at a constant rate, as observed with small solutes. Rather, these proteins were suddenly released into the adjoining PPP cells in distinct pulses (Figure 5, Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 5 and Video 3.

claim: Batch unloading did not occur at the same time into all cells, but independently into individual cells.
source: Batch unloading did not occur at the same time into all cells, but independently into individual cells (Figure 5; Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5 and Video 3.

claim: Small proteins such as GFP were batch unloaded and subsequently moved freely throughout the root.
source: Small proteins such as GFP were batch unloaded and subsequently moved freely throughout the root (Figure 5A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 5A-F.

claim: Large probes such as aequorin-GFP and SEOR-YFP became trapped inside the phloem-pole pericycle after batch unloading.
source: However, large probes such as aequorin-GFP and SEOR-YFP became trapped inside the PPP after batch unloading (Figure 5G–J; Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 5G-J and Video 4.

claim: Induction of callose in the phloem-pole pericycle using pCALS8::icals3m resulted in a significant arrest in primary root growth.
source: After callose induction we observed a significant arrest in primary root growth relative to roots that were transferred to a non-inducing medium (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 8 hr induction with pCALS8::icals3m, CF was restricted to protophloem sieve element files with minimal lateral unloading into the root.
source: Control roots showed the characteristic unloading pattern of wild-type plants (Figure 6C, n = 22) while induced plants showed a severe restriction in phloem unloading. At 8 hr induction, CF was restricted to PSE files with minimal lateral unloading into the root (Figure 6D, n = 20).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: At 24 hr induction with pCALS8::icals3m, CF did not enter the unloading zone and remained completely restricted to protophloem sieve elements distal to the unloading zone.
source: At 24 hr induction, this effect was even stronger. CF did not enter the unloading zone and remained completely restricted to PSEs distal to the unloading zone (Figure 6E, n = 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 6E.

claim: CF transport in psAPL::icals3m seedlings was unloaded without restriction at both 8 hr and 24 hr after estradiol induction.
source: As above, CF transport in these seedlings was monitored at 8 hr and 24 hr after estradiol induction. At both time points CF was unloaded without restriction, and induced and non-induced seedlings showed an identical pattern of unloading (Figure 6H–J, n = 3, n = 3, n = 2, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 6H-J.

claim: Callose induction in the psAPL::icals3m seedlings did not significantly affect root growth relative to the uninduced control plants.
source: Furthermore, we found that callose induction in the psAPL::icals3m seedlings did not significantly affect root growth relative to the uninduced control plants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Callose was deposited strongly in the phloem-pole pericycle relative to other cells surrounding the protophloem sieve element files in pCALS8::icals3m seedlings.
source: Confocal imaging of pCALS8::icals3m seedlings confirmed that callose was deposited strongly in the PPP relative to other cells surrounding the PSE files (Figure 6L–O)
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 6L-O.

claim: psAPL::icals3m roots showed strong callose labelling in the companion cell files.
source: while psAPL::icals3m roots showed strong callose labelling in the CC files, as predicted (Figure 6—figure supplement 6P–S).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6P-S.

claim: Phloem unloading occurs predominantly via the phloem-pole pericycle, not companion cells.
source: Collectively, these data provide strong evidence that phloem unloading occurs predominantly via the PPP, not CCs, and suggest that the PD between PSE and PPP are central players in the unloading process.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the callose induction experiments.

claim: Plasmodesmata between protophloem sieve elements and phloem-pole pericycle are central players in the unloading process.
source: Collectively, these data provide strong evidence that phloem unloading occurs predominantly via the PPP, not CCs, and suggest that the PD between PSE and PPP are central players in the unloading process.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the callose induction experiments.

claim: Plasmodesmata between protophloem sieve elements and metaphloem sieve elements were simple, or occasionally branched.
source: PD between the PSE and MP were simple, or occasionally branched (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Between protophloem sieve elements and companion cells, plasmodesmata displayed the typical single pore on the protophloem sieve element side and multiple branches towards the companion cell.
source: Between PSEs and CCs, PD displayed the typical single pore on the PSE side and multiple branches towards the CC (Figure 7C), as shown often for connections between SEs and CCs in other tissues (Esau and Thorsch, 1985; Oparka and Turgeon, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 7C and citations to previous studies.

claim: Most plasmodesmata between protophloem sieve elements and phloem-pole pericycle were funnel-shaped with apertures of up to 300 nm diameter at the protophloem sieve element entrance, tapering towards the phloem-pole pericycle entrance.
source: In addition to a few simple PD (10%; n = 20), funnel-shaped PD with apertures of up to 300 nm diameter were found at the PSE entrance, tapering towards the PPP entrance (Figure 7D–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations shown in Figures 7D-H.

claim: Serial block-face scanning electron microscopy collected 2100 serial transverse sections that spanned six complete sieve elements.
source: Using this method, we collected 2100 serial transverse sections that spanned six complete SEs (Figure 8A), including the junction between PSE zero and the adjacent immature PSE (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the SBFSEM method and reference to Figures 8A and B.

claim: Plasmodesmata relative distribution was 45.3%, 40.8%, and 13.9% between protophloem sieve element-phloem-pole pericycle, protophloem sieve element-companion cells, and protophloem sieve element-metaphloem sieve element, respectively, when corrected for the total interface between the cell types.
source: PD relative distribution was 45.3%, 40.8%, and 13.9% between PSE-PPPs, PSE-CCs, and PSE-MSE, respectively, when corrected for the total interface between the cell types.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of 3D reconstructions.

claim: The total number of plasmodesmata averaged 527 ± 58 (n = 4) per protophloem unloading domain.
source: We found that the total number averaged 527 ± 58 (n = 4) per protophloem unloading domain (since Arabidopsis roots are diarch, twice the number is available for unloading within the entire root tip).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of plasmodesmata counts.

claim: In the phloem-unloading zone of the root there are approximately 240 plasmodesmata at the protophloem sieve element-phloem-pole pericycle interface, 215 plasmodesmata at the protophloem sieve element-companion cell interface, and 73 plasmodesmata at the protophloem sieve element-metaphloem interface potentially available for unloading.
source: Based on the percentage distributions of PD obtained using serial sectioning, we calculated that in the phloem-unloading zone of the root there are approximately 240 plasmodesmata at the PSE-PPP interface, 215 plasmodesmata at the PSE-CC interface, and 73 plasmodesmata at the PSE-MP interface potentially available for unloading.
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from the measured PD distributions.

claim: The average phloem flow velocity in the protophloem translocation zone was measured to be 22.6 ± 5.1 µm/s (n = 11).
source: We measured the average phloem flow velocity in the protophloem translocation zone to be u = 22.6 ± 5.1 µm/s (n = 11)
evidence: The claim is based on direct measurements reported in the text.

claim: The average sieve tube diameter was measured to be 3.6 ± 0.44 µm (n = 11).
source: and the average sieve tube diameter to be: d = 3.6 ± 0.44 µm (n = 11)
evidence: The claim is based on direct measurements reported in the text.

claim: The volume flow rate to be unloaded from a single protophloem sieve element file is 230 femtoliter/s (230 µm3/s).
source: resulting in a volume flow rate of Q=π4d2u= 230 femtoliter/s (230 µm3/s) to be unloaded from a single PSE file.
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from measured parameters.

claim: Literature values on phloem sucrose concentration average about 500 mM.
source: Literature values on phloem sucrose concentration average about 500 mM (Hall and Baker, 1972; Kallarackal et al., 1989); Mendoza-Cózatl et al., 2008; Winter et al., 1992)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The required pressure differential to drive unloading solely by bulk flow through simple plasmodesmata would be 8.14 MPa.
source: We found that the required pressure differential to drive unloading solely by bulk flow through simple PD would be 8.14 MPa (see Appendix for detailed calculations).
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical modeling calculations.

claim: Assuming funnel plasmodesmata instead of simple plasmodesmata, the required pressure would be as low as 0.05–0.2 MPa.
source: However, assuming funnel PD instead of simple PD, the required pressure would be as low as 0.05–0.2 MPa.
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical modeling calculations.

claim: A concentration difference of 276 mM would be required for diffusive unloading through funnel plasmodesmata.
source: For the geometrical and physiological values listed above, a concentration difference of 276 mM would be required for diffusive unloading through funnel PDs.
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical modeling calculations.

claim: The distinctive funnel shape of the sieve element-to-phloem-pole pericycle plasmodesmata is crucial to enabling efficient unloading.
source: Our analysis of unloading kinetics leads us to conclude that the distinctive funnel shape of the SE-to-PPP PD is crucial to enabling efficient unloading.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the mathematical modeling and structural analysis.

claim: Convective phloem unloading (a combination of diffusion and bulk flow) is feasible with relatively moderate pressure and concentration differentials.
source: In this case, convective phloem unloading, i.e. a combination of diffusion and bulk flow, is feasible, and that relatively moderate pressure and concentration differentials are necessary to drive transport.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the mathematical modeling.

claim: Bulk flow is likely to be the dominant mechanism of unloading based on structural and physiological data.
source: Based on our structural and physiological data bulk flow is likely to be the dominant mechanism of unloading.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined structural and physiological data.

claim: Bulk flow would require a pressure differential of about 0.05–0.2 MPa, equal to an osmotic potential difference of about 20–80 mM.
source: Bulk flow would require a pressure differential of about 0.05–0.2 MPa, equal to an osmotic potential difference of about 20–80 mM.
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical modeling calculations.

claim: Solute unloading by diffusion alone would require a concentration difference of 276 mM.
source: Solute unloading by diffusion alone, on the other hand, would require a concentration difference of 276 mM.
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical modeling calculations.

claim: The protophloem sieve element-phloem-pole pericycle interface is the principal route for all solutes to be unloaded.
source: Our results indicate that the PSE-PPP interface is the principal route for all solutes to be unloaded.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Unlike the xylem pole pericycle, which is involved in lateral-root formation and apoplastic xylem loading, a specific role for the phloem-pole pericycle has not been proposed.
source: Unlike the xylem pole pericycle (XPP), which is involved in lateral-root formation (Parizot et al., 2012) and apoplastic xylem loading (Takano et al., 2002), a specific role for the PPP has not been proposed, although its transcriptome shares similarity to the underlying protophloem (Parizot et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents a gap in knowledge.

claim: The 'post-phloem domain' previously described by Stadler et al. (2005) and Paultre et al. (2016) is the phloem-pole pericycle.
source: We have now identified the 'post-phloem domain' previously described by Stadler et al. (2005) and Paultre, et al., 2016 as the PPP.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental identification of the PPP as the recipient of unloaded proteins.

claim: The phloem-pole pericycle may function as a repository for degraded protophloem sieve element contents as well as systemic macromolecules.
source: It appears that while the XPP may be involved in apoplastic xylem loading, the PPP is intimately involved in symplastic phloem unloading, and may function as a repository for degraded PSE contents as well as systemic macromolecules.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observed accumulation of macromolecules in the PPP.

claim: Phloem-pole pericycle cells may be specialized for the degradation of proteins and RNAs.
source: PPPs are the major recipients of systemic macromolecules and it might be expected that they are specialized for the degradation of proteins and RNAs, an interesting area for future research.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the potential function of PPP cells.

claim: Phloem-pole pericycle cells may protect the downstream cells from receiving unwanted, potentially interfering mRNA molecules.
source: PPPs may also protect the downstream cells from receiving unwanted, potentially interfering mRNA molecules.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the potential protective function of PPP cells.

claim: Phloem-mobile viruses are able to move beyond the phloem-pole pericycle.
source: Phloem-mobile viruses are able to move beyond the PPP suggesting that they can break the 'barrier' normally imposed by the PPP (Valentine et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Valentine et al., 2004.

claim: CalS8 is expressed specifically in the phloem-pole pericycle.
source: During the course of this study, we found that CalS8 is expressed specifically in the PPP (Figure 6A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 6A and B.

claim: Within the phloem unloading zone the sAPL promoter was expressed strongly in companion cells and metaphloem sieve element, but not in the phloem-pole pericycle.
source: Within the phloem unloading zone the psAPL promoter was expressed strongly in CCs and MSE, but not in the PPP (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 6F and G.
